newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: War of words intensifies in Serbian protest crisis.
newsitem.headline: War of words intensifies in Serbian protest crisis.

text.p: Signs of Serbian government authority faltering from relentless street protests increased on Friday when an eminent former ally of President Slobodan Milosevic accused him of ignoring the popular will.

There was no let-up in Serbia's marathon political crisis as thousands of people demonstrating against the government's annulment of municipal elections won by an opposition coalition marched again in Belgrade on Friday.

Signs of dwindling state authority spread with lawyers going on strike, teachers picketing and Belgrade university deans breaking off contacts with the pro-Milosevic rector who has resisted student demands to quit.

Three hundred members of the Belgrade Bar Association rallied to demand the resignation of the justice and interior ministers for their role in frustrating opposition efforts to have election results reinstated.

Street protests buffeting Serbia for almost three months have wrought dissension in the leftist establishment and the latest influential figure to break ranks was Borisav Jovic, once Milosevic's close associate.

Jovic, a former Yugoslav federal president who fell out with Milosevic over the rising power of the Serbian leader's wife, said in a British newspaper interview the policy of ignoring election results had divided and weakened the government.

He was quoted by the Guardian newspaper as urging Milosevic to admit election defeats in accordance with the law and reduce the clout of his wife Mira Markovic, who heads one of the governing parties, the Yugoslav United Left (JUL).
"If someone thinks they can do anything against ... the constitution and the law, that is a very serious situation," Jovic said in the interview, conducted in Belgrade.
Jovic blamed the crisis largely on the sway of Markovic, who has been vocally contemptuous of the opposition pro-democracy movement while Milosevic has remained silent.

"The problem is that Milosevic is elected by the people but she is not elected by anybody ... In practical terms, a lot of decisions are made by her. That is a completely abnormal situation," Jovic told the Guardian.

Jovic was chairman of old Yugoslavia's collective presidency in 1990-91 when the federation of six republics disintegrated amid rising Serb nationalism whipped up in large part by Milosevic and himself.

Current Yugoslav federal President Zoran Lilic betrayed doubt within governing circles when he said on Thursday that the crisis was caused in part by "dishonourable behaviour by individuals" who supervised the elections.

The informed newsletter VIP said Lilic lent support to the idea of reinstating the vote outcome at a meeting of the Main Board of Milosevic's Socialist Party (SPS) in the presence of the Serbian president last week.
Milosevic often uses Lilic as a mouthpiece for political "trial balloons" and VIP said the SPS Main Board would meet again this weekend to decide on steps to defuse the crisis.
Milosevic's wife lambasted Serbia's opposition coalition on Friday, accusing them in her regular magazine column of disrupting ordinary life and undermining the economy.

Markovic, the most despised figure in Serbia's ruling circle among opposition activists, said Zajedno protests had paralysed public transport, forcing people to walk home in mid-winter cold, and obstructed business contacts.
Friday was the 76th consecutive day of street rallies across Serbia since the November 17 election outcome in 14 of the republic's 18 biggest cities was nullified.
Investigators from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) have concluded that the balloting, nullified over murky unspecified "irregularities", was fair.
Socialist authorities lashed out at widening dissent by threatening to cut off cash for schools and universities that have been shut down by striking teachers and students.

Results of an independent opinion poll published on Friday showed that 12 percent of all Serbians over 18 years old, or roughly 700,000 people, were demonstrating on average every day in towns across the country.
The poll released by the Institute for Social Sciences also found that the number of voters backing Milosevic's coalition had shrunk by one third since November.
